why: Its 3300 K surface boils in granules about 295 km across, each living about 4 minutes, about 1653 across the star; larger cells about 7 thousand km wide, lasting about 18 hours, sweep its magnetic field into a net of about 13730 cells.
Its outer layer turns over in 58.2 days and it spins in 4.4: Rossby number 0.075, so saturated: heavily spotted, flaring constantly; X-rays are 7.4e-4 of its power (3.69e21 W).
Saturated stars show no clean cycle; their activity is steady and high.
stand_ins: granules are ten pressure scale heights across and live half a crossing time; supergranules 25 granules across with flows a fifth of the granule speed; convective speed from flux with a fixed photospheric opacity (all fitted on the Sun)
regime words: active above 10⁻⁴ of the star's power in X-rays, moderate above 3×10⁻⁷, quiet below (labels only; the numbers carry the physics)
spot coverage scales as the square root of the X-ray fraction from the Sun's 0.3 %, capped at half the disc

references.text: Trampedach, R., Asplund, M., Collet, R., Nordlund, Å. and Stein, R. F. 2013, A grid of three-dimensional stellar atmosphere models of solar metallicity. I. General properties, granulation, and atmospheric expansion, ApJ 769, 18: granule size scales with the surface pressure scale height across the grid.
Schwarzschild, M. 1975, On the scale of photospheric convection in red giants and supergiants, ApJ 195, 137: cell size follows the pressure scale height, so giants' cells are huge.
Nordlund, Å., Stein, R. F. and Asplund, M. 2009, Solar surface convection, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 6, 2: granules about 1 to 2 Mm across living minutes, with upflows of a few km/s near the surface.

Freytag, B., Steffen, M. and Dorch, B. 2002, Spots on the surface of Betelgeuse: results from new 3D stellar convection models, Astron. Nachr. 323, 213: red supergiants have only a few giant convection cells across their faces.

Rieutord, M. and Rincon, F. 2010, The Sun's supergranulation, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 7, 2: cells about 30 Mm across, lifetimes one to two days, horizontal flows about 300 to 400 m/s, outlined by the magnetic network.
Gray, D. F. and Nagel, T. 1989, The granulation boundary in the H-R diagram, ApJ 341, 421: no granulation in stars hotter than about early F.

Wright, N. J., Drake, J. J., Mamajek, E. E. and Henry, G. W. 2011, The stellar-activity-rotation relationship and the evolution of stellar dynamos, ApJ 743, 48: log τ = 1.16 − 1.49 log(M/M☉) − 0.54 log²(M/M☉) days (0.09 to 1.36 M☉); saturated log(L_X/L_bol) = −3.13 below Ro = 0.13; slope β = −2.70 above it (unbiased sample); Sun log(L_X/L_bol) = −6.24.

Noyes, R. W., Hartmann, L. W., Baliunas, S. L., Duncan, D. K. and Vaughan, A. H. 1984, Rotation, convection, and magnetic activity in lower main-sequence stars, ApJ 279, 763: activity depends on the Rossby number.

why: 3 flares above 3.0e24 J in 0.08 years; ten times the energy comes about a tenth as often.
stand_ins: flare durations scale as E^0.39 from 600 s at 10²⁵ J; rise is a tenth of decay
flare light is a 10000 K black body plus 10 % extra in soft X-rays; no radio burst yet

ejection share, speed and mass grow with flare energy by stated power laws; cone half-width 30°, leaving from over the flare's active region (anywhere within 30° of the equator in a spell with none); planets on circular orbits in that equator

references.text: Vasilyev, V. et al. 2024, Sun-like stars produce superflares roughly once per century, Science: (8.63 ± 0.20)×10⁻³ per year above 10³⁴ erg for 5000 to 6500 K stars with rotation over 20 days; energy spread dN/dE ∝ E^(−1.97 ± 0.30), consistent with the Sun's own flares extrapolated.
Shibayama, T. et al. 2013, Superflares on solar-type stars observed with Kepler I, ApJS 209, 5: dN/dE ∝ E^(−2.0) for slow rotators, −2.2 for all G dwarfs; fast rotators flare far more often.
Shibayama, T. et al. 2013, Superflares on solar-type stars observed with Kepler I, ApJS 209, 5: flare light as a 10 000 K black body.

Yashiro, S. et al. 2006, Different power-law indices in the frequency distributions of flares with and without coronal mass ejections, ApJ 650, L143: the share of flares with ejections rises with flare size, to nearly all of the largest.
